title: You launched it. But where did it land?
text: Medium You launched it. But where did it land? | by Bridal Pearson | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Press enter or click to view image in full size Product Strategy Product Management Leadership Customer Experience Innovation You launched it. But where did it land? Bridal Pearson 2 min read · Oct 31, 2026 -- Listen Share You launched it. But where did it land? A former leader once told me there’s a difference between launching a product and landing it. That distinction has stayed with me for years. But lately, I’ve found myself asking another question: how do we know we’re trying to land in the right place? Now, getting something out the door deserves some celebration. The dependencies alone… 😂 Anyone who has worked through a launch knows what it takes. But I’ve been thinking about this even earlier in the process, while working through a strategy. There are opportunities that make sense on paper. Customer habits suggest a fit. Competitors are already doing something in the space. You can connect the dots and build a reasonable case. Okay, there’s something here. But where do we start? With whom? And what would make this valuable enough for them to use? Seeing someone else pursue an opportunity can give us a reason to investigate. It doesn’t tell us which customer need we’re best positioned to address — or what we might discover along the way. That’s part of what I enjoy about strategy. You develop a point of view, then work out how to test it. The starting point can change as the evidence gets clearer. The tricky part is that, as we build the strategy, we also build a case for it. We secure support, commit resources, and explain why this is the direction to take. By the time customers get their hands on it, we can be pretty invested in how the story is supposed to end. So when their behavior looks different, “we need to drive adoption” can become a convenient explanation. Maybe we do. Maybe the experience needs work or the value isn’t clear. But are we also looking for what their behavior might be telling us about the opportunity itself? I remember hearing the Post-it story early in my product career. An adhesive found a use as a bookmark, then exchanging messages on the sticky paper helped reveal something bigger. Imagine being so focused on improving the bookmark that you overlooked what people were doing with the notes. Every unexpected signal won’t warrant a pivot. We still have to investigate, test, and exercise judgment. But if every result leads to “keep going,” what would it actually take to change our minds? I still believe there’s a difference between launching and landing… It’s just that I’m less convinced we should always land where we originally intended. Hmmmm. What are your thoughts?
